PROJECT 1
Cold-Gas Reaction Thruster

A platform that rotates and holds its heading by firing puffs of compressed gas —
exactly like a spacecraft's RCS

Cost: ~$75
Difficulty: Advanced
Build Time: 2-3 weekends
Why This Matters

Out in orbit there is nothing to push against, so spacecraft change and hold their orientation by firing
small thrusters — the reaction control system (RCS). You can build the same thing on the ground:
mount a platform on a near-frictionless bearing, plumb a few small solenoid valves to a
compressed-gas supply, and fire short puffs to rotate it and hold a commanded heading. An IMU
senses the angle, a controller decides which thruster to pulse and for how long, and the platform slews
and stops on target — no wheels, no contact, just gas. This is exactly how satellites maneuver, and the
air-bearing version is literally how aerospace labs test real attitude-control hardware before flight. It is
the most viscerally 'spacecraft' project you can build on a bench.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand reaction-control propulsion, closed-loop attitude
control, solenoid valve driving and pulse-width thrust modulation, and inertial sensing. Propulsion
and GNC are core spacecraft disciplines, and demonstrating thruster-based attitude control on an air
bearing is exactly the kind of hardware aerospace teams build and test.

→ The job this maps to: spacecraft propulsion and GNC — satellite and launch companies, and the
air-bearing test labs that validate attitude-control systems.

Safety: Compressed gas is genuinely dangerous. Use only a properly rated regulator and tubing,
never exceed component pressure ratings, and secure the gas supply so it cannot become a
projectile. Use inert gas (CO2 or filtered compressed air) — never anything flammable or an
unregulated high-pressure source — wear eye protection, and fully depressurize before working on
the plumbing.
@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Build a Real Satellite   •   Page 3
How It Works

• Newton's third law in a vacuum: A spacecraft cannot push against anything, so it carries its own
reaction mass: expel gas one way, the body rotates the other. Firing a thruster offset from the
center of mass produces a torque that slews the vehicle. Your bench version does the identical
thing on a low-friction bearing that mimics the freedom of orbit.

• Near-frictionless bearing: The platform sits on a ball bearing, a lazy-Susan, or — for the stretch
version — a planar air bearing that floats it on a thin film of air. The lower the friction, the more the
demo behaves like a real satellite, where the only torques are the ones you command.

• Solenoid 'thrusters': Small 12 V solenoid valves act as on/off thrusters. Mounted in opposing pairs
at the platform's edge and fed from a regulated gas line, each releases a puff of gas through a
nozzle when energized. Opposing pairs let you torque clockwise or counter-clockwise.

• Pulsed thrust control: You cannot throttle a solenoid, so you modulate thrust the way real RCS does
— by pulse width and pulse frequency. Short pulses give fine control near the target; longer or more
frequent pulses give a fast slew. The controller translates a commanded torque into a valve on-time.

• Closed-loop attitude control: An IMU measures the platform's angle and rate; a PD controller
computes the torque needed to reach and hold the setpoint, then thruster-selection logic fires the
correct valve. Because gas is limited, the controller must avoid a 'limit cycle' — chattering around
the target and wasting gas — which is a real spacecraft design problem.
@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Build a Real Satellite   •   Page 4
Key Design Decisions
→ Why cold gas instead of anything fancier? Cold-gas propulsion — just releasing a pressurized

inert gas — is the simplest, safest thruster there is, and it is genuinely flown on small satellites. No
combustion, no high voltage, no toxic propellant: ideal for learning the control problem without the
hazards of real rocketry.
→ Why pulse-width modulate thrust? A solenoid valve is on or off; it cannot be partly open in a

controllable way. Spacecraft RCS solves this with pulse modulation — varying how long and how
often you fire — mapping a continuous torque command onto discrete puffs. Tuning it is the heart of
the project.
→ Why an air bearing for testing? Aerospace labs validate attitude-control hardware on air-bearing

tables precisely because they remove friction and gravity torque, leaving the vehicle free to rotate
as it would in orbit. Building even a simple version teaches you how flight hardware is actually
tested on the ground.

Build Steps

Build the frictionless platform: Mount a rigid disk on a low-friction bearing (a quality lazy-Susan to
start, a planar air bearing for the stretch build). Balance it carefully so gravity introduces no torque — it
should sit still at any angle when undisturbed.

Plumb the gas system: Fit a regulator to the gas supply and run rated tubing to opposing solenoid
valves at the rim, each ending in a small nozzle. Keep supply pressure within every component's
rating, and leak-check before powering anything.
@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Build a Real Satellite   •   Page 5

Wire valves + IMU: Drive each solenoid from a MOSFET with a flyback diode (valves are inductive).
Mount the IMU at the platform's center and read angle and rate over I2C. Confirm a brief valve pulse
produces a clean puff and a small rotation.

Close the control loop: Implement a PD controller: from heading error and rate, compute a torque
command, then convert it to a valve and a pulse width. Add a deadband so the platform does not fire
constantly near the target — that is how you stop wasting gas in a limit cycle.

Slew and hold on camera: Command a 90-degree turn and film the platform puffing gas, rotating, and
stopping precisely on the new heading. Nudge it and watch it fire to recover. Log angle vs. time to show
the slew and settle — the language of attitude control.
Interview Questions:
→ How does a reaction-control thruster change a spacecraft's orientation with no external
reference?
→ Why is thrust modulated by pulse width and frequency rather than throttling the valve?
→ What is a limit cycle in RCS control, and why does it waste propellant?
→ Why are air-bearing tables used to test attitude-control hardware on the ground?
→ Why is cold-gas propulsion attractive for small satellites despite its low performance?
→ How would you allocate thruster firings for combined slew and disturbance rejection?

PROJECT 2
Auto-Tracking Ground Station
A motorized antenna that locks onto a satellite and physically follows it across the sky

Cost: ~$70
Difficulty: Advanced
Build Time: 2-3 weekends
Why This Matters

A satellite in low orbit crosses the sky in minutes, so to keep a high-gain antenna pointed at it you need
a tracker that moves. This project builds a real azimuth-elevation rotator: two motors aim an antenna, a
microcontroller predicts the satellite's position from its orbital elements, and the antenna physically
slews to follow the pass from horizon to horizon — exactly what a professional ground station does.
Pair it with an SDR and you can hold a lock on a fast-moving satellite and pull down a clean signal a
fixed antenna would lose in seconds. It is the ground half of every space mission, and watching your
antenna hunt across the sky on its own is genuinely striking.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand satellite tracking and orbital prediction
(TLEs/SGP4), azimuth-elevation pointing and motor control, antenna gain and link geometry, and
ground-station automation. The ground segment is a huge part of the space industry, and a working
auto-tracker is a concrete TT&C; and RF skill.

→ The job this maps to: ground segment and TT&C; (telemetry, tracking & command) — satellite
operators, ground-station networks, and RF/antenna teams.
@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Build a Real Satellite   •   Page 7
How It Works

• Predicting where the satellite is: Every tracked satellite has published orbital elements (a TLE —
two-line element set). An SGP4 propagator turns those plus the current time into the satellite's
position, which is then converted to an azimuth (compass bearing) and elevation (angle above the
horizon) from your exact location.

• Azimuth-elevation rotator: Two motors — one for azimuth, one for elevation — aim the antenna at
any point in the sky. Geared steppers (or DC motors with position feedback) move the antenna to
the commanded az/el and update continuously as the satellite moves.

• Why a moving antenna at all: A high-gain, directional antenna has a narrow beam, which is what
gives it the gain to hear a weak satellite — but that beam must stay pointed. A fixed antenna trades
gain for coverage; a tracker gives you both by following the target.

• Closing the loop with the SDR: An SDR at the feed receives the downlink while the rotator tracks.
Because the satellite moves fast, you also correct for Doppler shift in software. Accurate pointing
plus Doppler correction keep a solid lock across the whole pass.

• Horizon-to-horizon automation: The controller waits for a predicted pass, slews to the rise point
(AOS), tracks across the sky, and parks at the set point (LOS) — fully automatic. A scheduler can
chain multiple satellites across a day, exactly like an operational ground station.

Build Steps

Build the az-el rotator: Construct a two-axis mount: an azimuth base that spins the whole assembly
and an elevation axis that tilts the antenna up. Use motors with enough torque to hold the antenna
steady, and add end stops or position feedback.

Mount a directional antenna: Build or attach a lightweight VHF/UHF Yagi as the payload. Balance it
on the elevation axis so the motor is not fighting gravity. Run the feedline with a service loop so the
cable does not bind as the rotator turns.

Run SGP4 on the controller: Load the target satellite's TLE and implement SGP4 (libraries exist for
most MCUs). Feed it your location and the current time; verify it outputs az/el that matches a tracking
app for the next pass.

Drive the motors to az/el: Map the computed az/el to motor positions and update once a second.
Calibrate the azimuth zero to true north and the elevation zero to the horizon. Watch the antenna track
a 'virtual' pass before trying a real one.

Track a live pass + receive: Connect the SDR, wait for a real pass, and let the station track from AOS
to LOS. Apply Doppler correction in the SDR software and capture the downlink. Film the antenna
sweeping the sky on its own — the money shot.
Interview Questions:
→ What is a TLE, and how does SGP4 turn it into a pointing direction?
→ Why does a high-gain antenna require active tracking while an omni does not?
→ How do you convert a satellite's predicted position into azimuth and elevation for your site?
→ Why must you correct for Doppler shift during a low-orbit pass?
→ How do you calibrate the rotator's azimuth and elevation references?
→ What limits your tracking accuracy, and how would you improve it?

PROJECT 3
Magnetorquer Detumble System

Coils that push against Earth's magnetic field to stop a tumbling platform — how a
CubeSat stabilizes after launch

Cost: ~$30
Difficulty:
Intermediate-Advanced
Build Time: 1-2 weekends
Why This Matters

When a CubeSat is ejected from its deployer it is tumbling, and before it can do anything useful it has
to stop spinning and stabilize — a maneuver called detumbling. The clever part: it has nothing to push
against, so it pushes against Earth itself. Electromagnets called magnetorquers create a magnetic
moment that interacts with Earth's magnetic field to produce a tiny torque, bleeding off the spin. This
project builds exactly that: coils on a platform, a magnetometer to sense rotation, and the famous
'B-dot' control law that drives the coils to kill the tumble. It is one of the most elegant ideas in spacecraft
engineering — steering against a planet's magnetic field — and it is genuinely buildable and cheap.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand magnetic actuation, the B-dot detumbling control
law, magnetometer sensing and the geomagnetic field, and coil/driver design. Magnetorquers are
flown on most CubeSats, and demonstrating detumbling control is a direct, recognizable ADCS skill.

→ The job this maps to: spacecraft attitude control (ADCS) — CubeSat and smallsat companies, and
ADCS subsystem teams.
@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Build a Real Satellite   •   Page 10
How It Works

• Pushing against a planet: A magnetorquer is just a coil; running current through it creates a
magnetic dipole. That dipole tries to align with Earth's magnetic field — like a compass needle —
producing a torque on the spacecraft. With no reaction mass needed, it is an almost-free way to
control attitude in low orbit.

• Sensing the tumble: A 3-axis magnetometer measures Earth's field in the spacecraft's frame. If the
spacecraft is rotating, that measured field vector sweeps around — and the rate at which it changes
(its derivative) tells you how fast you are tumbling. This is the key insight behind the control law.

• The B-dot control law: B-dot drives each coil proportional to the rate of change of the measured field
(the 'B-dot' signal), in the direction that opposes the change. The result is a torque that always fights
the tumble, smoothly bleeding off rotational energy until the field stops sweeping. It needs no
knowledge of absolute orientation, which is why it is so robust.

• Driving the coils: An H-bridge per axis lets the controller push current either direction through each
coil, so it can torque whichever way is needed. Coil current sets the dipole strength; the bigger the
coil and current, the more torque — traded against power and heat.

• Demonstrating it on the ground: Hang the platform on a thin thread (a torsion pendulum) or float it
on a bearing, give it a spin, and watch the B-dot controller drive the coils to slow and stop it relative
to Earth's field. The same algorithm runs on real CubeSats minutes after deployment.

Build Steps

Wind the magnetorquers: Wind three air-core coils (or coils on a ferrite rod for more moment) on the
three axes of a small frame. More turns and area give more magnetic moment per amp. Measure each
coil's resistance and confirm it produces a field with a compass.

Read the magnetometer: Mount the 3-axis magnetometer away from the coils and read all three axes
over I2C. Rotate the platform by hand and watch the field vector sweep — confirming you can sense
rotation.

Drive coils with H-bridges: Wire each coil to an H-bridge so the MCU can energize it in either
polarity. Verify a commanded current produces a deflection near a reference magnet, and that you can
reverse the torque direction.

Implement B-dot: Compute the derivative of the measured field, then set each coil's current opposite
to that rate of change. Tune the gain so it responds firmly without chattering. Crucially, pulse the coils
and read the magnetometer when they are off, so you measure Earth's field, not your own coils.

Detumble on a thread: Suspend the platform on a thin thread or float it on a bearing, spin it up, and
switch on B-dot. Watch the rotation slow and settle. Log angular rate vs. time to show the exponential
detumble — the exact curve a CubeSat produces in orbit.
Interview Questions:
→ How does a magnetorquer produce torque without any reaction mass?
→ What does the magnetometer's rate of change tell you about the spacecraft's motion?
→ Explain the B-dot control law and why it does not need absolute attitude knowledge.
→ Why must you sense the field with the coils de-energized?
→ What are the limitations of magnetic actuation — when can't it control an axis?
→ How do magnetorquers complement reaction wheels in a full ADCS?

PROJECT 4
Satellite-in-a-Box Flight Computer

An avionics stack that reads its sensors and beams CCSDS-style telemetry packets
down to a ground dashboard

Cost: ~$50
Difficulty:
Intermediate-Advanced
Build Time: 2-3 weekends
Why This Matters

Every spacecraft has a brain: the command-and-data-handling (C&DH;) computer that reads the
sensors, runs the housekeeping, packages everything into telemetry, and beams it to the ground while
accepting commands back up. This project builds a working one — a flight-computer stack that
samples its sensors, forms proper telemetry packets, transmits them over a radio link to a ground
station you also build, and decodes them onto a live dashboard. Use the real spacecraft data standard
(CCSDS) for the packets and you have built the same data architecture that flies on actual missions. It
is less flashy than a thruster, but it is the literal nervous system of a satellite — and the flight-software
skill is in high demand.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand command-and-data-handling architecture,
telemetry packetization (CCSDS), reliable serial/radio links, and ground-side decoding and display.
Flight software and C&DH; are central to every space mission, and a working telemetry pipeline is a
standout systems project.

→ The job this maps to: command & data handling (C&DH;) and flight software — satellite primes,
CubeSat companies, and avionics teams.
@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Build a Real Satellite   •   Page 13
How It Works

• The C&DH; role: The flight computer is the spacecraft's housekeeper: on a fixed schedule it reads
every sensor (voltages, currents, temperatures, attitude), checks system health, stores data, and
assembles telemetry for downlink — all while listening for commands from the ground. It is the
integration point for every other subsystem.

• Housekeeping telemetry: Your stack samples a set of 'housekeeping' channels — battery voltage,
board temperature, IMU attitude, a packet counter — at a steady rate. This is exactly the data
operators watch to know a real satellite is alive and healthy.

• CCSDS packetization: Spacecraft do not send raw numbers; they wrap data in standardized
packets. The CCSDS space-packet format adds a header (identifying the data type, a sequence
count, a timestamp) and a checksum. Implementing it means your telemetry is structured,
parseable, and corruption-checkable — the way flight data really works.

• The radio link: A simple radio module (a UHF data module, or LoRa for easy range) carries the
packet stream to the ground. You frame the packets for the link, and the ground side detects frame
boundaries, validates checksums, and rejects corrupted packets — the reliability layer every
downlink needs.

• Ground decoding + dashboard: On the ground, software receives the stream, parses the CCSDS
packets back into named values, and plots them live — voltages trending, temperature rising,
attitude changing. Add a command uplink and you can send instructions back, completing a real
telemetry-and-command loop.

Build Steps

Bring up the sensors: Wire the IMU, a temperature sensor, and a voltage/current monitor to the flight
MCU. Sample them on a fixed schedule (say 1 Hz) and confirm clean readings. These are your
housekeeping channels.

Build CCSDS packets: Implement the CCSDS space-packet structure: a primary header with an
application ID, a sequence counter, and a timestamp, then your sensor payload, then a checksum.
Print the raw bytes and verify the structure by hand before transmitting.

Add the radio downlink: Connect a radio module and frame the packets for it (sync word + length +
packet + CRC). Transmit at a steady rate. On the second radio at the ground, capture the framed bytes
and confirm you are receiving the stream.

Decode on the ground: Write ground software that finds frame boundaries, validates the CRC, parses
the CCSDS header and payload, and prints named telemetry. Reject and count corrupted packets so
you can see link quality.

Build the dashboard + uplink: Plot the telemetry live (a simple web dashboard or plotting script) —
voltage, temperature, attitude, packet count. Add a command uplink so the ground can change a
setting on the flight computer. Demonstrate the full loop end to end.

PROJECT 5
Sun-Vector Sensor

A photodiode-array sensor that computes the exact direction to the Sun — the
most-flown attitude sensor in space

Cost: ~$25
Difficulty: Intermediate
Build Time: 1 weekend
Why This Matters

To point itself, a spacecraft first has to know which way it is facing — and the simplest, cheapest,
most-flown way to get a reference is to find the Sun. A sun sensor measures the direction to the Sun in
the spacecraft's own frame, and that single vector is enough to constrain attitude for power-positioning
and coarse pointing. This project builds a real one: an arrangement of photodiodes (or a pinhole over a
small sensor array) whose relative readings encode the Sun's angle, plus the math to turn those
readings into a sun vector. It is a clean, satisfying sensor project — analog front end, geometry, and
calibration — and it is a genuine flight sensor, not a toy.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand optical attitude sensing, photodiode analog
front-ends and ratiometric measurement, the geometry of converting intensities into an angle, and
sensor calibration. Sun sensors fly on nearly every satellite, and building one is a recognizable
ADCS sensing skill.

→ The job this maps to: attitude determination (ADCS) — CubeSat and satellite companies, and
sensor/ADCS subsystem teams.
@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Build a Real Satellite   •   Page 17
How It Works

• Why the Sun: The Sun is a bright, effectively point source in a known direction, making it the easiest
celestial reference to measure. Knowing the sun vector in the body frame lets a spacecraft orient its
solar panels and perform coarse attitude control — which is why almost every satellite carries a sun
sensor.

• Photodiodes at angles: If you mount photodiodes facing slightly different directions (or put a single
pinhole/mask over a small array), each receives sunlight at a different incidence angle. Since a
photodiode's output falls off predictably with angle (roughly as the cosine), the relative outputs
depend on where the Sun is.

• Ratiometric measurement: Absolute brightness varies with distance and conditions, so you do not
use raw values — you use ratios between diodes. Ratios cancel overall intensity and depend only
on the angle, which is the trick that makes the sensor robust. This is the same principle as
commercial analog sun sensors.

• Analog front end: Each photodiode's tiny current is converted to a voltage by a transimpedance
amplifier and read by the MCU's ADC. Matching the channels and keeping noise low matters,
because the angle accuracy comes directly from how cleanly you measure the photocurrents.

• Computing the sun vector: From the calibrated ratios, the MCU computes the two angles that
define the Sun's direction (azimuth and elevation in the sensor frame), outputting a unit vector.
Calibrating against known Sun angles turns the raw geometry into an accurate sensor.

Build Steps

Arrange the photodiodes: Either tilt four photodiodes outward in a shallow pyramid, or place a
pinhole mask above a quad photodiode so the light spot shifts with Sun angle. Both encode direction
into the relative outputs; the pinhole approach is more precise.

Build the analog front end: Convert each photodiode current to a voltage with a transimpedance
amplifier using matched feedback resistors. Read all channels on the MCU's ADC. In shade, confirm
near-zero; in sun, confirm strong, sensible readings.

Take ratios, not raw values: Compute ratios between opposing channels so overall brightness
cancels. Verify that moving a light source (or tilting the sensor toward the Sun) changes the ratios
smoothly and repeatably while brightness changes do not.

Calibrate against known angles: Point the sensor at the Sun (or a collimated lamp) at several known
angles and record the ratios. Fit a simple model mapping ratios to angle — this calibration is what turns
the device into a real sensor.

Output the sun vector: Use the calibrated model to output the Sun's azimuth and elevation, or a unit
vector, live on the OLED. Demonstrate it tracking the Sun's direction as you rotate the sensor — and
discuss its accuracy and field of view.
Interview Questions:
→ Why is the Sun the most common attitude reference for spacecraft?
→ Why use ratios of photodiode outputs instead of absolute intensities?
→ How does a photodiode's output depend on the angle of incoming light?
→ What does the transimpedance amplifier do, and why does channel matching matter?
→ How do you calibrate raw readings into an accurate angle?
→ What are a sun sensor's limitations (eclipse, albedo, field of view)?

PROJECT 6
CubeSat Power System (EPS)

Solar input, battery management, regulated distribution, and power telemetry — a real
satellite's electrical heart

Cost: ~$45
Difficulty:
Intermediate-Advanced
Build Time: 2 weekends
Why This Matters

A satellite lives and dies by its power system. The EPS (electrical power subsystem) harvests energy
from solar panels, charges and protects the battery, regulates it into the voltage rails every other
subsystem needs, and reports power health as telemetry — all of it autonomously, because there is no
one to flip a switch in orbit. This project builds a real one: a solar input stage that charges a lithium
battery safely, regulated output rails, protection against over-current and over-discharge, and
voltage/current telemetry on every channel. It is the same architecture as a flight EPS, and it is the
subsystem that keeps everything else alive — which is exactly why power engineers are always in
demand.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand solar energy harvesting, lithium battery charging
and protection, DC-DC regulation and power distribution, and power telemetry/monitoring. The EPS
is mission-critical on every spacecraft, and building one demonstrates real power-electronics and
systems competence.

→ The job this maps to: electrical power systems (EPS) — satellite and CubeSat companies, and
power-electronics subsystem teams.
@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Build a Real Satellite   •   Page 20
How It Works

• Harvesting solar power: Solar cells are the only energy source in orbit, but their output swings with
sun angle and temperature. The charge stage (often with MPPT, as in the solar-controller project)
extracts as much power as conditions allow and uses it to charge the battery.

• Battery charging + protection: A lithium battery must be charged within strict voltage and current
limits and protected against over-charge, over-discharge, over-current, and temperature extremes
— any of which can damage or destroy it. The EPS enforces all of this automatically; in space there
is no replacing a cooked battery.

• Regulated distribution: Different subsystems need different, clean voltages (e.g. 3.3 V for logic, 5 V
for radios). DC-DC converters generate these regulated rails from the battery, and the EPS
distributes them — often with the ability to switch individual loads on and off.

• Protection and autonomy: Each rail has over-current protection so one faulty subsystem cannot pull
down the whole bus, and the battery has an under-voltage cutoff so the satellite can safely 'brown
out' and recover. This autonomy is essential — the spacecraft must protect itself.

• Power telemetry: The EPS measures voltage and current at the solar input, the battery, and each
rail, and reports them as telemetry. Operators watch this to understand the energy balance — is the
satellite generating more than it consumes? — one of the most important health metrics of any
mission.

Build Steps

Build the charge stage: Wire the solar panel to a lithium charge-controller IC sized for your cell,
ideally with an MPPT input stage. Confirm it charges the battery from sunlight within the correct
voltage/current limits and stops at full charge.

Add battery protection: Use a protected cell or add a protection board enforcing over-charge,
over-discharge, and over-current limits. Test the under-voltage cutoff by loading the battery down and
confirming it disconnects safely.

Generate regulated rails: Add buck converters for 3.3 V and 5 V from the battery. Verify each rail is
clean and holds voltage under load. These are the rails the rest of your 'satellite' would run on.

Instrument every channel: Place INA-class voltage/current monitors on the solar input, the battery,
and each rail, and read them on the MCU. Now you can see exactly where power is flowing and how
much.

Add switching + telemetry: Add high-side load switches so the MCU can turn rails on and off, and
stream all the power telemetry (with over-current protection) to a display or your flight computer.
Demonstrate the energy balance: solar in vs. load out, charging and discharging.

Six subsystems. One satellite.
Build them and you've built the real thing.

Propulsion, attitude control, attitude sensing, flight software, ground systems, and power. Put these six
together and you do not have six gadgets — you have the functional subsystems of an actual satellite,
built on a bench for the price of a textbook each. A thruster that slews a platform, coils that detumble
against Earth's field, a sun sensor, a flight computer streaming telemetry, a tracking ground station,
and a power system to keep it all alive. That is genuinely how spacecraft are organized, and how space
companies hire.

The space industry recruits by subsystem — GNC, ADCS, propulsion, C&DH;, ground, EPS — and a
working demo of any one of these speaks that language directly. You are not claiming to have built a
satellite; you are showing you can build the part they need.

Build even one of these. Log the slew, plot the detumble curve, screenshot the telemetry dashboard,
show the energy balance. Put it on your GitHub with a proper README and the subsystem it maps
to. You will have a portfolio piece that puts you in the room with a real space-hardware team.

spacecraft.
